concept.name: Load, Soak & Spike Testing

relationships.description: Connects Load, Soak & Spike Testing to contract testing in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Load, soak, and spike testing validate how a system behaves under sustained target throughput, multi-hour resource pressure, and sudden traffic cliffs using realistic protocol mixes and open-workload generators.
spark.keyTakeaway: Load tests prove capacity, soak tests expose slow leaks, and spike tests reveal autoscaling lag and queue collapse before customers do.

concept.whyItMatters: Functional tests pass at 1 RPS while production failures happen when connection pools saturate, GC pauses compound, or 10x traffic arrives faster than Kubernetes HPA can boot pods. Distinguishing steady-state capacity (load), time-dependent degradation (soak), and burst resilience (spike) prevents blind capacity planning and p99 tail-latency collapses.
whenToUse: Before major releases, schema migrations, or infrastructure changes (e.g., TLS 1.3 or HTTP/2 upgrades) that alter CPU, memory, or connection-pool footprints.
Ahead of predictable traffic cliffs such as flash sales, ticket drops, or market-open bursts where arrival rates jump 5x–20x in under 30 seconds.
When qualifying long-lived stateful services (Kafka consumers, gRPC streaming servers, JVM microservices) for memory leaks, file-descriptor exhaustion, or connection drift.
whenNotToUse: As a substitute for unit or contract tests when core business logic or serialization schemas are still unstable.
Directly against shared production databases or third-party payment/SMS APIs without isolated sandboxes or wire-level mocks.
With closed-loop VU scripts that wait for each response before sending the next request when you actually need to measure open-world arrival rates.
keyPoints: Open-model workload generators (k6 constant-arrival-rate, Vegeta, Gatling `constantUsersPerSec`) decouple request arrival rate from server latency, avoiding Coordinated Omission.
Load tests ramp smoothly (e.g., 500 to 5,000 RPS over 15 minutes) to map the knee of the throughput-vs-p99 latency curve.
Soak (endurance) tests hold 70%–85% of peak load for 8–72 hours to catch 2–5 MB/hour heap leaks, unclosed HikariCP connections, or WAL/log-disk fill.
Spike tests inject sudden step-changes (e.g., 1,000 to 12,000 RPS in 10 seconds) to test rate limiters, circuit breakers, and pod cold-start headroom.
Synthetic payloads must mirror production distributions (Zipfian hot keys, payload sizes, cache-hit ratios, and think times) rather than a single static `GET /health`.

examples.title: E-Commerce Checkout Flash-Sale Qualification
examples.scenario: A checkout service handles 800 RPS normally but expects 9,000 RPS within 20 seconds at midnight during a sneaker drop.
examples.outcome: A spike test in k6 exposed a 55-second EKS HPA + JVM warmup lag and HikariCP `connectionTimeout` exhaustion at 3,200 RPS, prompting pre-warmed standby replicas and an Envoy token-bucket edge limiter.

examples.title: 72-Hour Soak Test on a gRPC Telemetry Ingestor
examples.scenario: A Go/gRPC ingestion service passed 30-minute load tests at 15,000 RPS with 18 ms p99 latency.
examples.outcome: A 48-hour soak at 11,000 RPS uncovered a 1,200-goroutine/hour leak on canceled client streams, causing RSS to hit the 4 GiB cgroup OOMKill limit at hour 38.

tradeOffs.pro: Multi-hour soak tests catch slow resource leaks, log-rotation stalls, and DB table bloat that short runs miss.
tradeOffs.con: Long runs delay CI/CD pipelines and burn significant cloud load-generator and staging environment cost.

tradeOffs.pro: Open models (fixed arrival rate) reveal true queueing explosions and tail latency when the server slows down.
tradeOffs.con: They can rapidly overwhelm fragile staging environments if generators lack max-VU caps and abort thresholds.

tradeOffs.pro: Full-stack staging with realistic data cardinality surfaces lock contention, index misses, and DNS/NAT bottlenecks.
tradeOffs.con: Mirroring multi-terabyte databases and third-party dependencies is expensive and operationally complex to reset between runs.

failureModes.name: Coordinated Omission
failureModes.description: Closed-loop virtual users pause sending new requests while waiting on a slow response, artificially hiding 5-second GC stalls from p99 histograms.
failureModes.mitigation: Use open arrival-rate executors (`constant-arrival-rate` in k6 or HdrHistogram correction) and track intended vs. actual send timestamps.

failureModes.name: Load Generator Bottleneck
failureModes.description: The test runner saturates its own ephemeral ports (`TIME_WAIT` exhaustion), CPU, or TLS handshake capacity before the target service hits its limit.
failureModes.mitigation: Monitor generator CPU, NIC drops, and socket counts; distribute runners across multiple nodes and tune `net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range`.

failureModes.name: Unrealistic Cache Hit Inflation
failureModes.description: Repeating the same 100 user IDs yields a 99.9% Redis hit rate during testing, masking a catastrophic PostgreSQL collapse under production Zipfian cardinality.
failureModes.mitigation: Seed staging with production-scale row counts and drive requests from a shuffled Zipfian or production-replay key distribution.

failureModes.name: Autoscaler & Cold-Start Blindness
failureModes.description: Gradual 30-minute ramps allow HPA and JVM JIT compilers to scale smoothly, giving false confidence for sudden 15-second real-world spikes.
failureModes.mitigation: Run dedicated step-spike profiles from cold baseline and measure error budgets during the entire scale-out window.

commonMistakes: Testing only average or p50 latency instead of p95/p99/p99.9 and error rates.
Running against a nearly empty database where every index fits in RAM and sequential scans look fast.
Leaving client-side timeouts infinite or unset so slow calls pile up without triggering realistic retry storms.
Forgetting to warm up JIT, connection pools, or CDN caches—or conversely, only testing after everything is artificially pre-warmed.
Skipping automated pass/fail SLO thresholds in CI, turning performance tests into ignored dashboards.

sections.content:
## The idea

Performance failures rarely come from a single slow line of code; they emerge from nonlinear queueing behavior under Little's Law (`L = λ · W`) and time-dependent resource drift. Load, soak, and spike testing are three distinct experimental lenses on the same distributed system:

- **Load testing** measures steady-state capacity and latency across a controlled ramp (e.g., 500 → 5,000 RPS) to locate the saturation knee where p99 latency diverges.
- **Soak (endurance) testing** holds sustained load (typically 70%–85% of peak) over 8–72 hours to surface slow leaks in heap, native memory, goroutines, file descriptors, or database vacuuming.
- **Spike testing** applies instantaneous step increases (e.g., 5x–15x baseline in < 30 s) to verify admission control, circuit breakers, retry budgets, and autoscaler reaction time.

## Concrete walkthrough

Consider qualifying a Go + PostgreSQL + Redis order API targeting 2,500 RPS steady state and 10,000 RPS burst:

1. **Baseline & Shape**: Capture production traffic mix (65% `GET /orders/{id}`, 25% `GET /catalog`, 10% `POST /orders`), payload sizes (1.2–4.8 KB), and Zipfian key skew (`α = 1.1`).
2. **Load Ramp (45 min)**: Use k6 `ramping-arrival-rate` from 500 to 4,000 RPS. At 2,900 RPS, PostgreSQL `HikariCP` / `pgxpool` wait time jumps from 2 ms to 85 ms, defining the safe operating ceiling at ~2,400 RPS.
3. **Spike Injection (15 min)**: Hold 1,000 RPS for 5 min, jump to 10,000 RPS for 90 s, then drop back to 1,000 RPS. Verify Envoy sheds excess load with `429 Too Many Requests` within 200 ms rather than letting queues build 30-second timeouts, and confirm recovery within 60 s after the burst ends.
4. **Soak Run (24 hr)**: Hold 2,000 RPS continuously while scraping Prometheus (`go_goroutines`, `process_resident_memory_bytes`, `pg_stat_activity`). Any monotonic slope in RSS or open sockets fails the release gate.

sections.content:
## Workload models & queueing math

Understanding why systems collapse requires pairing **open-model** injection with **Little's Law** (`L = λ · W`) and **Amdahl/Universal Scalability Law (USL)**.

- **Closed vs. Open**: In a closed model with 200 VUs, if p99 latency jumps from 20 ms to 2,000 ms, throughput automatically drops because VUs sit blocked. In an open model, `λ` stays at 2,000 RPS; concurrency `L` balloons from 40 to 4,000 in-flight requests, exhausting worker threads and heap.
- **Retry Amplification**: If 10% of requests time out and clients retry 3 times with jitter-free backoff, effective `λ` spikes by 1.3x–3x right at the saturation knee, turning a recoverable blip into a metastable failure.

## Comparing load, soak & spike profiles

| Dimension | Load Test | Soak (Endurance) Test | Spike Test |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Primary Question** | What is our max sustainable RPS within p99 SLO? | Do leaks or bloat degrade performance over time? | Do rate limiters and autoscalers survive sudden bursts? |
| **Traffic Shape** | Stepped ramp (e.g., 20% → 120% peak) | Flat sustained plateau (70%–85% peak) | Instant step-up (5x–15x in 5–30 s) then drop |
| **Typical Duration** | 15–60 minutes | 8–72 hours | 5–20 minutes |
| **Key Signals** | Saturation knee, p99 curve, CPU/DB pool | RSS/heap slope, FD count, autovacuum lag | 429/503 ratio, HPA scale time, recovery time |
| **Common Culprit Found** | Missing index, undersized pool, N+1 query | Connection/goroutine leak, disk/WAL fill | Retry storm, cold-start OOM, lock convoy |

## Failure modes

1. **Metastable Retry Storms**: Timeouts trigger immediate client retries, doubling arrival rate when the backend is already above 90% utilization. *Mitigation*: Enforce exponential backoff with full jitter and per-hop retry budgets (e.g., Envoy `retry_budget: 20%`).
2. **Ephemeral Port Exhaustion**: High-churn HTTP/1.1 connections leave thousands of sockets in `TIME_WAIT` on either the runner or NAT gateway. *Mitigation*: Enable HTTP/2 multiplexing or keep-alive pooling and widen `ip_local_port_range`.
3. **Slow-Burn Memory & Descriptor Leaks**: A 3 MB/hour leak passes every 30-minute load test but OOMKills pods in production every 16 hours. *Mitigation*: Run automated overnight 12-hour soak tests with linear regression checks on heap/RSS.
4. **Autoscaler Thrashing**: Metrics scraping lag (15–30 s) plus container startup (30–60 s) means spikes hit before pods are ready. *Mitigation*: Pre-warm headroom buffers, use request-concurrency-based scaling (KEDA/Knative), and shed excess at the edge.

## Telemetry, tooling & CI integration

Treat performance testing like a controlled lab experiment:

- **Tooling**: Use **k6** or **Gatling** for scenario-rich HTTP/gRPC/WebSocket flows, **Vegeta** for high-RPS open-loop stateless blasts, and **Locust** when Python business logic is needed.
- **Telemetry Alignment**: Correlate runner HdrHistogram metrics (`http_req_duration{p(99)}`) with server-side RED/USE metrics (Rate, Errors, Duration; Utilization, Saturation, Errors) using a shared `test_run_id` tag.
- **CI Gating**: Run a 5-minute smoke load test on every PR merge to `main`, a 45-minute full load + spike suite nightly, and a 24-hour soak test on release candidates.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Define explicit SLO pass/fail thresholds (e.g., `p99 < 120 ms`, `5xx < 0.1%`, `RSS slope < 1 MB/hr`).
- [ ] Configure open-arrival-rate executors to prevent Coordinated Omission.
- [ ] Seed staging data to production-like row counts and Zipfian key distributions.
- [ ] Monitor load-generator CPU, RAM, and `TIME_WAIT` sockets so the runner never becomes the bottleneck.
- [ ] Test both ramp-up saturation (load), 12–72 hr endurance (soak), and 10x sudden bursts (spike) with post-spike recovery verification.

interviewProblems.title: Load, Soak & Spike Testing
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Load, Soak & Spike Testing. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

simulation.title: Interactive Simulation: Load Soak Spike Testing

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Load, soak, and spike testing validate how a system behaves under sustained target throughput, multi-hour resource pressure, and sudden traffic cliffs using realistic protocol mixes and open-workload generators.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: API Cluster & Pool applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Telemetry & SLO Gate.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Telemetry & SLO Gate experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Use open arrival-rate executors (`constant-arrival-rate` in k6 or HdrHistogram correction) and track intended vs. actual send timestamps.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Load tests prove capacity, soak tests expose slow leaks, and spike tests reveal autoscaling lag and queue collapse before customers do.
Avoid trap: Testing only average or p50 latency instead of p95/p99/p99.9 and error rates.
Avoid trap: Running against a nearly empty database where every index fits in RAM and sequential scans look fast.
When to reach for it: Before major releases, schema migrations, or infrastructure changes (e.g., TLS 1.3 or HTTP/2 upgrades) that alter CPU, memory, or connection-pool footprints.
When to reach for it: Ahead of predictable traffic cliffs such as flash sales, ticket drops, or market-open bursts where arrival rates jump 5x–20x in under 30 seconds.

putItTogether.title: Putting Load Soak Spike Testing Together
putItTogether.summary: Load tests prove capacity, soak tests expose slow leaks, and spike tests reveal autoscaling lag and queue collapse before customers do.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Load Soak Spike Testing before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: A spike test in k6 exposed a 55-second EKS HPA + JVM warmup lag and HikariCP `connectionTimeout` exhaustion at 3,200 RPS, prompting pre-warmed standby replicas and an Envoy token-bucket edge limiter.
